name: Nova Scotia
summary_text: Nova Scotia stands under the national framework of Canada. Gender identity and gender expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and under the hate-motivation provisions of the Criminal Code, both added by Bill C-16, which the Senate passed 67-11 in June 2017, and courts have applied those protections consistently. No jurisdiction in Canada restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities. Federal criminal law and human-rights protections apply uniformly in Nova Scotia.  Legal gender recognition operates largely on self-declaration. Most provinces allow the gender marker on official documents to be changed by declaring one's identified gender; Prince Edward Island's 2016 amendment to its Vital Statistics Act removed the prior surgery requirement and replaced it with a declaration supported by a doctor's letter. Federally, identity documents can carry an X marker. Entry into Canada carries no trans-specific friction.  Correctional placement is the weakest point in the Nova Scotia record. The Chronicle Herald reported on 18 March 2025 that a federal judge gave a transgender woman from the Halifax region more time to file her application for judicial review of the decision to hold her in a men's prison while she serves a two-year robbery sentence. The judge cited a lack of transparency and clear, timely communication in the institutional decision-making, and systemic barriers that restricted the applicant's access to her lawyer. Federal policy after Bill C-16 is that transgender prisoners are to be placed according to their gender identity, so the case turns on whether that policy is being applied in the province's custodial system.  Nova Scotia's provincial government operates an explicit inclusion framework rather than restrictive trans-specific legislation. On 8 January 2026 it released the province's first 2SLGBTQIA+ Action Plan, developed under the Dismantling Racism and Hate Act passed in 2022, described as the first Canadian law of its kind to explicitly acknowledge 2SLGBTQIA+ people, and informed by more than 600 community members through surveys, virtual meetings and consultations. On 10 June 2026 the province announced more than $176,000 through the first round of its 2SLGBTQIA+ Community Impact Grant program.  National hate-crime data does not resolve trans-specific risk in the province. Statistics Canada reported on 30 March 2026 that 4,882 police-reported hate-crime incidents were recorded nationally in 2024, 1% above 2023, at a national rate of 12.1 per 100,000, down 2% in 2024 and up 142% since 2018, with eight provinces recording stable or declining rates. The release carries no Nova Scotia-specific rate or incident count, and it breaks out sexual orientation as a motivation category rather than gender identity, so trans-specific hate-crime volume is not established by this dataset.

sources.title: Criminal Code Section 159 and repeal via Bill C-32 / Bill C-75
